chapters.name: Chapter 1: Thinking like a data analyst

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What data science is, and the five steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name the five steps of a data project and match them to a real example.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real question, such as a coach's or a shop's, you will list the five steps of a data project in order and match each to the example, with all five steps (Ask, Get, Clean, Explore, Share) in the right order.
Data science means using data to answer questions and make better decisions. Data analysis is the hands-on part: cleaning, counting, comparing and charting.
Almost every project follows five steps. Ask: what do you want to know? Get: find the data. Clean: fix mistakes and gaps. Explore: count, average, compare and chart. Share: tell people what you found in plain words.
Example: a youth soccer coach asks "Do we score more in the second half?" She gets the scores from each game, cleans out a game that was cancelled, adds up first-half and second-half goals, and shares a simple chart with the team.
Step by step:
- Ask a clear question.
- Get the data.
- Clean it.
- Explore it with counts, averages and charts.
- Share what you found.
Words to know:
- Data: facts and numbers collected about something.
- Data science: using data to answer questions and guide decisions.
- Data analysis: cleaning, summarizing and charting data to find answers.
- Dataset: a collection of data, usually a table.
Try it now: Think of one question from your own life, work or community that data could answer (for example "Which day do I spend the most?"). Write what you would do at each of the five steps.
You can now describe the five steps of a data project and plan one.

check.q: What happens in the Clean step of a data project?
options: You fix mistakes and gaps in the data
check.why: Clean means fixing mistakes and gaps before you explore.

check.q: A shop owner asks, "Which day do we sell the most?" What would you do right after this Ask step?
options: Average the days of the week
Get the sales data with dates
check.why: After Ask comes Get: find the data that can answer the question.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Knowing your data: rows, columns and types
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read a data table and say what each column holds and what type it is.
This lesson builds toward: Given a data table and a question, you will describe what each column holds and its type and check whether the data can answer the question, naming numeric and categorical columns correctly and saying so when a question cannot be answered.
Most data comes as a table. Tidy data means each row is one thing you measured (one game, one sale, one person) and each column is one fact about it (date, amount, team).
Columns have types. Numbers you can do math with, like price or minutes. Categories are groups, like day of the week or team name: you count them, but you do not average them. Dates are their own type.
Good questions match the data you have. "What is the average sale on Saturdays?" needs a sale amount column and a day column. If the data does not have it, you cannot answer it, and saying so is part of the job.
Step by step:
- Say what one row stands for.
- List each column and what it means.
- Mark each column as number, category or date.
- Check that your question can be answered with these columns.
Words to know:
- Row: one record: one thing you measured.
- Column: one fact recorded for every row.
- Tidy data: one row per thing, one column per fact.
- Numeric: a column of numbers you can do math with.
- Categorical: a column of groups or labels, like day or team.
Try it now: Make a small table of your last 7 days: date, day of the week, hours of sleep and mood from 1 to 5. Label each column as number, category or date, and write one question the table can answer and one it cannot.
You can now read a table, name each column's type and check whether a question fits the data.

options: A column of groups, such as team name or day of the week
check.why: Categories are groups you count, not average.

check.q: Your sales table has amount and day columns but no time of day. Someone asks if mornings sell more. What would you say?
options: The data cannot answer that, because there is no time column
check.why: If the data does not have it, you cannot answer it, and saying so is part of the job.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Averages, outliers and not being fooled
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out the mean and median, spot an outlier, and avoid a common mistake.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short list of numbers or a claim about two things, you will calculate the mean and median, identify any outlier and check whether a claim mixes up correlation and cause, with the mean and median correct and every correlation-cause mix-up named.
The mean (average) is the total divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value when you sort them. For 3, 4, 4, 5 and 34 the mean is 50 / 5 = 10, but the median is 4.
That 34 is an outlier: a value far from the rest. It might be a typo, or it might be real and important. Outliers pull the mean a lot but barely move the median, so when there are outliers, the median often describes a typical value better.
Two things moving together is called correlation, but it does not prove that one causes the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer: the sun causes both. Before you claim a cause, look for another reason.
Step by step:
- Sort the numbers.
- Mean: add them and divide by how many.
- Median: take the middle one (or the average of the two middle ones).
- Look for values far from the rest and check whether they are mistakes.
- Before saying "X causes Y", look for another explanation.
Words to know:
- Mean: the average: total divided by count.
- Median: the middle value when the numbers are sorted.
- Outlier: a value far from the others.
- Correlation: two things that tend to move together.
- Causation: one thing actually making another happen.
Try it now: Here are 7 delivery times in minutes: 22, 25, 19, 24, 95, 21, 23. Work out the mean and the median by hand, name the outlier, and write which number better describes a typical delivery and why. (Mean about 32.7, median 23.)
You can now calculate a mean and median, spot outliers and avoid mixing up correlation and causation.

check.q: What is the mean of 2, 4, 6 and 8?
Bus wait times this week were 5, 6, 5, 7 and 60 minutes. Which number would you report as a typical wait?
check.why: The 60 is an outlier that pulls the mean up; the median shows a typical wait.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Loading and looking at data with pandas
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Load a dataset into a pandas DataFrame in Colab and describe it.
This lesson builds toward: In Google Colab with pandas, you will load a dataset into a DataFrame and describe its rows, columns and types, using head(), shape, info() and describe() and reporting the results correctly.
pandas is a free Python library for working with tables, and it is already in Google Colab. A table in pandas is called a DataFrame, usually named df.
For practice we use a real restaurant dataset of 244 meals that comes with seaborn, a charting library: df = sns.load_dataset("tips"). It needs internet, which Colab has. Its columns include total_bill, tip, day, time (Lunch or Dinner) and size (people at the table). For your own data, pd.read_csv("file.csv") loads a CSV file you upload.
Four commands show you what you have: df.head() shows the first five rows, df.shape gives rows and columns, df.info() lists each column's type, and df.describe() gives the count, mean, min, max and more for the number columns.
Step by step:
- In a new Colab notebook run: import pandas as pd and import seaborn as sns
- Load: df = sns.load_dataset("tips")
- Look: df.head()
- Size and types: df.shape and df.info()
- Summary: df.describe()
Words to know:
- pandas: a free Python library for working with tables of data.
- DataFrame: a table in pandas, with rows and named columns.
- CSV: a plain text file of a table, with commas between values.
- head(): shows the first rows of a DataFrame.
- describe(): gives summary numbers for each number column.
Official sources:
- pandas: 10 minutes to pandas
- seaborn: load_dataset
- Google Colab: Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Load the tips dataset in Colab. Write down how many rows and columns it has, which columns are numbers and which are categories, and the mean and maximum total_bill from df.describe().
You can now load a dataset with pandas and describe its size, columns and summary numbers.

check.why: df.info() lists each column and its type.

check.q: You uploaded your club's file attendance.csv to Colab. Which line would you use to load it?
check.why: pd.read_csv loads a CSV file you upload.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Cleaning, filtering and grouping
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check for missing values, add a column, filter rows and compare groups.
This lesson builds toward: Given a loaded DataFrame, you will check for missing values, add a calculated column, filter rows and compare groups, with each step's code running and any cleaning written down.
Clean first. df.isna().sum() counts missing values in each column. If some are missing, you can drop those rows with df.dropna() or decide how to fill them; write down what you did. Also check for impossible values, like a negative bill.
Make the column you need. A $5 tip means different things on a $20 bill and a $100 bill, so add a fair measure: df["tip_pct"] = df["tip"] / df["total_bill"] * 100.
Filter rows with a condition: df[df["time"] == "Dinner"] keeps only dinners. Group to compare: df.groupby("day")["tip_pct"].mean() gives the average tip percent for each day. If pandas prints a yellow warning, read it, but it is not an error. .round(1) makes the numbers neater.
Step by step:
- Count missing values: df.isna().sum()
- Add a column: df["tip_pct"] = df["tip"] / df["total_bill"] * 100
- Filter: dinners = df[df["time"] == "Dinner"]
- Group: df.groupby("day")["tip_pct"].mean().round(1)
- Try another group, like time or size.
Words to know:
- Missing value: an empty cell; pandas shows it as NaN.
- Cleaning: finding and fixing missing, wrong or impossible values.
- Filter: keep only the rows that match a condition.
- groupby: split rows into groups and summarize each group.
Official sources:
- pandas: 10 minutes to pandas
Try it now: Check the tips data for missing values. Add the tip_pct column. Find the average tip percent for each day and for Lunch versus Dinner. Write down which day had the highest average.
You can now check data for missing values, create a new column, filter rows and compare groups.

options: Drops rows that have missing values
check.why: dropna() removes rows with missing values; write down that you did it.

check.q: You see a bill of -12.00 in the data. What would you do?
options: Treat it as an impossible value, fix or remove it, and note what you did
Keep it; negative bills are normal
Average it with the others anyway
check.why: Check for impossible values like a negative bill as part of cleaning.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making a chart and sharing honest findings
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make a clear bar chart and write findings people can trust.
This lesson builds toward: Given your group results, you will make a titled bar chart and write findings that state their limits, with numbers from your own results and at least one honest limit.
A chart shows a pattern faster than a table. A bar chart is best for comparing groups: tip_by_day = df.groupby("day")["tip_pct"].mean() then tip_by_day.plot(kind="bar", title="Average tip % by day"). Give every chart a title and say what the numbers mean.
Write findings in plain sentences with the number: "On average, [day] tips were the highest, at about X percent of the bill." Use the number your own code printed.
Be honest about limits. Say how many rows a group has: df["day"].value_counts() shows a day with few meals, so its average is less reliable. This data came from one restaurant, so it may not hold for others. And it shows what happened, not why.
Step by step:
- Make the grouped numbers.
- Plot them: .plot(kind="bar", title="...")
- Check group sizes with value_counts().
- Write three findings with real numbers.
- Add one limit: what the data cannot tell you.
Words to know:
- Bar chart: a chart of bars used to compare groups.
- value_counts(): counts how many rows each group has.
- Finding: a clear statement of what the data shows, with a number.
- Limitation: something your data or analysis cannot tell you.
Official sources:
- pandas: 10 minutes to pandas
Try it now: Final task: in one notebook, load the tips data, check for missing values, add tip_pct, find the average tip percent by day and by time, make a bar chart of one of them with a title, and write three findings with numbers, including one thing this data cannot tell you.
You can now turn a dataset into a chart and honest, plain-language findings.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Loading and checking the data The data does not load, or missing values were not checked. The tips data is loaded, described and checked for missing values. Also notes the number of rows and the type of each column used. Tip percent column No tip percent column, or it is calculated wrongly. A tip_pct column equal to tip divided by total_bill times 100. Also checks for impossible values such as a negative bill. Group averages Only one comparison, or the averages are wrong. Average tip percent for each day and for lunch versus dinner, rounded. Also shows how many meals are in each group. Bar chart No chart, or the chart has no title. A bar chart of one comparison with a clear title. Axis labels or a note say what the numbers mean. Honest findings Fewer than three findings, or no limit stated. Three plain findings with numbers from the results, including one thing the data cannot tell you. Also avoids claiming a cause and mentions small groups where they matter. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which kind of chart is best for comparing groups, such as days?
options: A pie chart of one number
check.why: A bar chart is best for comparing groups.

check.q: Your chart shows Saturdays had higher tips. What would you add before sharing it?
options: A claim that Saturdays cause bigger tips everywhere
A made-up number to make it clearer
A title and an honest limit, such as how many meals each day had
check.why: A title and an honest limit help people trust and understand the finding.
